claims.claim: Hartlage says Curse of Strahd gives pages of room description to notable NPCs' homes and calls Chris Perkins's details creepy and moody while judging most of those rooms unreachable in play.
claims.quote: The homes of notable NPCs get pages of room descriptions.
claims.page: Matching description to a location's purpose

claims.claim: Hartlage reports that Curse of Strahd carries boxed text for every location while its successor Storm King's Thunder omits almost all read-aloud text.
Justin Alexander's judgment on the state of the form is that published adventures' location keys are almost all bad.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian
claims.quote: the location keys in published adventures are almost universally terrible

claims.claim: Alexander says a standardised section format pushes writers to fill every heading, so a Tactics section gets paragraphs even when the orcs have only swords.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian
claims.quote: it tends to encourage writers to “fill the format”

claims.claim: Alexander makes the order of a location description depend on the scene rather than a fixed template, contrasting a visible ogre with a hidden goblin.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian
claims.quote: A room with an ogre standing in the middle of it

claims.claim: Alexander dates the arrival of boxed text to Lost Tamoachan and says the prewritten descriptions appeared between quotation marks before TSR boxed them in the 1980 reissue.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian
claims.quote: the text was not yet boxed, instead appearing between quotation marks

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch diagnoses Lost Mine of Phandelver's generic feel as a failure of modifiers rather than of nouns and verbs.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, review of Lost Mine of Phandelver, tenfootpole.org
claims.quote: the adjectives and adverbs were not used very well

claims.claim: Lynch shows the cure as a single added modifier before a role noun and lists six alternatives that would each conjure a different woman.
claims.quote: the prim farmers wife tells you

claims.claim: Lynch's complaint about the Phandalin section is that the town's language is thin outside its core locations.
claims.quote: quite light on descriptive and evocative language

claims.claim: Lynch asks for a web of stated relationships among a town's named residents so the place exists apart from the party.
claims.quote: a web of personal relationships between the various people living in town

claims.claim: Lynch calls the one-sentence-per-NPC summary of who is in town, where they are and what they want invaluable and asks for more adventures to carry one.
claims.quote: That’s done in just a sentence or so each.

claims.claim: Lynch says a monster entry should tell the DM what the characters sense, and offers a smell and a coat as the missing kind of detail.
claims.quote: what the PC’s EXPERIENCE when they meet them

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch calls much of Curse of Strahd's read-aloud laughable and quotes single-sentence examples from it, among them one that names nothing at all.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, review of Curse of Strahd, tenfootpole.org, quoting Curse of Strahd
claims.quote: You find something on the ground.

claims.claim: Lynch's charge against Curse of Strahd's prose is a fixed inflation ratio, three sentences doing one sentence's work.
claims.quote: Three sentences are used when one will do.

claims.claim: Lynch credits Curse of Strahd with villages whose residents each have something going on, and says events attached to locations are what make the places feel alive.
claims.quote: The villagers and places, in particular, seem more alive

verdicts.note: Quote verbatim on the raw dmdavid.com tag page (full article text present). Page also carries “author Chris Perkins fills them with creepy, moody details” and, for unreachability, “players might explore some of these rooms” + “they will never enter the Burgomaster’s scullery” + “Often then, I realized that nothing would bring players to the location.” The page’s quantifier is “often/many”; “most” follows from “some” being the explored minority. All limbs supported.

Verbatim: “His follow-up, Storm King’s Thunder, omits almost all read-aloud text.” The other limb is on the same page: “Curse of Strahd includes it for every location.” Page says “follow-up” (Perkins’s next adventure) where the claim says “successor” — same substance.

Verbatim in the article’s third paragraph: “Which is why I find it fairly surprising that the location keys in published adventures are almost universally terrible.” Author/venue confirmed (The Alexandrian, ‘The Art of the Key’, May 19 2014).

Verbatim including curly quotes. The orc limb is the very next sentence: “You probably don’t really need to tell a DM that the orcs attack people using their swords (since that’s the only weapon they have)… but the format says you should have a ‘Tactics’ section, so you might as well write two or three paragraphs about it.” Under the ADVENTURE FORMATTING GUIDES heading, as cited.

Verbatim: “A room with an ogre standing in the middle of it should talk about the ogre first; a room with a goblin hiding behind a tapestry, on the other hand, shouldn’t lead off with the goblin.” The anti-template limb is supported by “This sort of one-size-fits-all formatting becomes both a straitjacket and an excess” and “a rigid adventure format forces information to be presented out-of-sequence.”

Verbatim under THE ERA OF BOXED TEXT. Page: boxed text “arrived for the first time in Lost Tamoachan: The Hidden Shrine of Lubaatum”; “In the original version of the module, the text was not yet boxed, instead appearing between quotation marks”; “But in 1980, TSR reissued the module as C1 The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan, placing the prewritten descriptions in a box for the first time.” All three limbs supported.

Verbatim: “There were nouns and verbs but the adjectives and adverbs were not used very well.” The generic-feel limb is in the same paragraph: “Hence the kind of ‘generic’ vibe. Generic goblin. Generic cave. Generic wolves.” Review confirmed as Bryce Lynch on Lost Mine of Phandelver.

Verbatim: “‘The farmers wife tells you … ’ instead of the ‘the prim farmers wife tells you …’”. Six alternatives counted on the page: “Granny, prim, biddy, lusty, stoic, proper”, of which the page says “They conjure a NON-generic image in your mind that you can build on” — the claim’s “each conjure a different woman” is that in other words.

Verbatim inside “The whole town is quite light on descriptive and evocative language/scenes outside of the core locations”, in the Part 2 town section as cited. Lynch immediately widens it — “(and, I will assert later, IN the core locations as well.)” — so the claim is narrower than the page, not at odds with it.

Verbatim: “I would have liked to see a web of personal relationships between the various people living in town.” Purpose limb verbatim too: “This will help make the town seem alive and to exist outside of the interactions of the party.” Page names residents by role (guild master, innkeeper, trading company) rather than by name.

Verbatim. Surrounding text carries every limb: “the adventure gives a brief summary of the major NPC’s, where they hang out, and what their objectives/quests are. That’s done in just a sentence or so each. I find these sorts of references INVALUABLE. … More adventures need to do this.”

Verbatim: “The monster descriptions are boring as hell, with almost no attention paid to what the DM actually needs: what the PC’s EXPERIENCE when they meet them.” The smell and the coat are the next two sentences: “Stink like the grave? Matted patchy fur? None of that is present.”

Verbatim, and inside the “On to the bad” section as cited (heading two paragraphs above). Page: “The read-aloud in this, in many places, is laughable”, then single-sentence examples — “You stumble upon an old grave.”, “You find a corpse.” — culminating in “Here’s a masterpiece of creative read-aloud writing!!! ‘You find something on the ground.’”, which names nothing.

verdicts.trueWording: Three sentences are used when one will do. Six are used when it needed two, or three.
verdicts.note: Quote is verbatim in the “On to the bad” section and the inflation charge is real (“the text is long/meaningless… the entries are so long that the important bits are lost… This is one of the major sins of the adventure”). But the page immediately supplies a second, different ratio, so Lynch offers illustrations of bloat, not a fixed ratio.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the charge is a fixed inflation ratio — the page's very next sentence gives a different one (“Six are used when it needed two, or three”)

verdicts.note: Verbatim: “The villagers and places, in particular, seem more alive than they have in many other WOTC/5E adventures…” Residents limb: “There are multiple people in each village who all have something going on with them. Each with their own personality.” Events limb: “This is then augmented by many of the locations having events… almost every location has one or two events… It brings the place to life. No longer static many of the villages now feel alive…”
